HPX provides a cheap\n`counting_iterator` that yields a sequence of integers (`0,1,2,…`).  \nUsing that iterator we can walk over the *indices* of the vector without\ncreating any temporary container.\n\nThe whole operation is expressed in a single call – no helper functions,\nno manual thread management – and the HPX runtime will split the work\namong the available cores using the `par` execution policy.\n\n---\n\n### Code\n\n```cpp\n#include <hpx/hpx_main.hpp>\n#include <hpx/parallel/algorithms/transform_reduce.hpp>\n#include <hpx/parallel/execution.hpp>\n#include <hpx/iterator_support/counting_iterator.hpp>\n\n#include <vector>\n#include <functional>   // std::multiplies\n\n/*  Return the product of the vector x with every odd‑indexed element inverted.\n    i.e.  x0 * 1/x1 * x2 * 1/x3 * … .\n    The computation is performed in parallel with HPX.\n*/\ndouble productWithInverses(std::vector<double> const& x)\n{\n    using namespace hpx::parallel;\n    using namespace hpx::parallel::execution;\n\n    // Counting iterators that generate the indices 0 … x.size()-1\n    auto first = hpx::util::counting_iterator<std::size_t>(0);\n    auto last  = hpx::util::counting_iterator<std::size_t>(x.size());\n\n    // Transform‑reduce:\n    //   * transform:   index → (even ? x[i] : 1.0/x[i])\n    //   * reduce:      multiplication\n    //   * init value:  1.0 (neutral element of multiplication)\n    return transform_reduce(\n        par,                     // execution policy – run in parallel\n        first, last,             // range of indices\n        1.0,                     // initial value (neutral element)\n        std::multiplies<double>{},   // reduction operation\n        [&](std::size_t i) -> double   // transformation lambda\n        {\n            double v = x[i];\n            // odd index → invert, even index → keep as‑is\n            return (i & 1u) ? 1.0 / v : v;\n        });\n}\n```\n\n---\n\n### Why this is fast\n\n| Aspect | Reason |\n|--------|--------|\n| **No temporaries** | The algorithm works directly on the original vector; only the index stream is generated on‑the‑fly. |\n| **Single pass** | `transform_reduce` fuses the map (invert‑odd) and the reduction (multiply) into one traversal, reducing memory traffic. |\n| **Work‑stealing scheduler** | The `par` policy lets HPX split the index range into chunks that are dynamically balanced across all cores, giving good scalability even for irregular workloads. |\n| **Cache‑friendly** | Each thread works on a contiguous block of indices, so accesses to `x[i]` are sequential and cache‑efficient. |\n| **Thread‑safe** | The reduction operator (`std::multiplies`) is associative and commutative, which HPX exploits safely in a parallel reduction. |\n\nThe function returns `1.0` for an empty vector (the neutral element of multiplication) and behaves correctly for any size of `x`. `std::transform_reduce` (C++‑17) that\n\n1. walks over a *range*,\n2. transforms each element,\n3. reduces the transformed values with a binary operator (here multiplication).\n\nThe only difficulty is that the transformation depends on the **index** of the element, not on the value alone.  \nHPX ships a `counting_iterator` that yields a sequence of indices (`0,1,2,…`).  \nBy iterating over those indices we can fetch `x[i]` inside the transform‑lambda and apply the “invert‑on‑odd‑index” rule.\n\nThe whole algorithm therefore reduces to a single call to `hpx::parallel::transform_reduce` with the `par` execution policy.\n\n---\n\n### Code\n\n```cpp\n#include <hpx/hpx_main.hpp>\n#include <hpx/parallel/algorithms/transform_reduce.hpp>\n#include <hpx/parallel/execution.hpp>\n#include <hpx/iterator_support/counting_iterator.hpp>\n\n#include <vector>\n#include <cstddef>   // std::size_t\n#include <functional> // std::multiplies\n\n/*  Return the product of the vector x with every odd indexed element inverted.\n    i.e.  x_0 * 1/x_1 * x_2 * 1/x_3 * x_4 ...\n    The computation is performed in parallel with HPX.\n    If the input vector is empty the neutral element of multiplication (1.0) is returned.\n*/\ndouble productWithInverses(std::vector<double> const& x)\n{\n    using namespace hpx::parallel;\n    using namespace hpx::parallel::execution;\n\n    // Empty vector → product = 1 (neutral element of multiplication)\n    if (x.empty())\n        return 1.0;\n\n    std::size_t const n = x.size();\n\n    // counting_iterator produces 0,1,2,…,n‑1\n    auto or 1/x[i])\n    //   - reduce   : multiply all terms together\n    double result = transform_reduce(\n        par,               // execution policy – run in parallel\n        first, last,       // range of indices\n        1.0,               // init value (neutral element of multiplication)\n        std::multiplies<>(), // reduction operation\n        [&](std::size_t i) // transform operation\n result;\n}\n```\n\n---\n\n### Why this is efficient\n\n| Aspect | Reason |\n|--------|--------|\n| **Parallelism** | `transform_reduce` with the `par` policy splits the index range into chunks that are processed by multiple HPX worker threads, fully utilizing the available cores. |\n| **Cache‑friendly** | The algorithm walks the vector **once** in order (via the index iterator). Each thread works on a contiguous sub‑range, giving good spatial locality. |\n| **No temporaries** | The transformation is performed on‑the‑fly; no auxiliary containers are allocated. |\n| **Reduced productWithInverses(std::vector<double> const& x)\n{\n    // Short‑circuit for an empty vector – the neutral element of multiplication.\n    if (x.empty())\n        return 1.0;\n\n    // Aliases for : 1.0/v\n    //   * reduction:       multiplication\n    //   * initial value:   1.0 (multiplicative identity)\n    double result = par::transform_reduce(\n        exec::par,                     // each element (here we read `x[i]` and possibly invert it),\n* combines the results with a **binary** operation (here multiplication).\n\nThe implementation below:\n\n* uses `boost::irange` to generate the index range `[0, x.size())`,\n* applies the required transformation in the unary lambda,\n* multiplies everything together with `std::multiplies<>`,\n* runs under the parallel execution policy `hpx::execution::par`.\n\nThe code is completely self‑contained, has no helper functions, and works for any size of `x` (including the empty vector, which correctly yields `1.0`).\n\n```cpp\n#include <hpx/hpx_main.hpp>\n#include <hpx/execution.hpp>\n#include <hpx/parallel/algorithms.hpp>\n\n#include <boost/range/irange.hpp>\n\n#include <vector>\n#include <functional>   // std::multiplies\n\n/* productWithInverses(std::vector<double> const& x)\n{\n    // Parallel transform‑reduce over the index range [0, x.size()).\n    //   * unary_op : fetch the element and invert it if the index is odd\n    //   * binary_op: multiplication\n    //   * init     : 1.0 (neutral element of multiplication)\n    return hpx::parallel::transform_reduce(\n        hpx::execution::par, The whole operation is performed with the\nparallel execution policy `hpx::parallel::execution::par`.\n\nThe implementation below is completely self‑contained, uses no helper\nfunctions, and follows HPX.\n    For an empty vector the neutral element of multiplication (1.0) is returned.\n*/\ndouble productWithInverses(std::vector<double> const& x)\n{\n    // Parallel execution policy\n    namespace const& tup)         // transformation lambda\n        {\n            const double val = boost::get<0>(tup);\n            const std::size_t idx = boost::get<1>(tup);\n            return (idx % 2 == 0) ? val : 1.0 / val;\n        });\n\n    return result;\n}\n```\n\n### Why this is efficient\n\n* **Work‑sharing** – `transform_reduce` automatically splits the range among\n  HPX threads, keeping all <hpx/parallel/algorithms/reduce.hpp>\n#include <hpx/execution.hpp>\n#include <boost/iterator/counting_iterator.hpp>\n#include <vector>\n#include <functional>   // std::multiplies\n\n/*  Return the product of the vector x with every odd indexed element inverted.\n    i.e.  x_0 * 1/x_1 * x_2 * 1/x_3 * x_4 ...\n    The computation is performed in parallel with HPX.\n    For an empty vector the neutral element of multiplication (1.0) is returned.\n*/\ndouble productWithInverses(std::vector<double> const& x)\n{\n    // Parallel execution policy (uses all available HPX threads)\n    auto exec counting_iterator<std::size_t> last (x.size());\n\n    // Parallel reduction:\n    //   - init value = 1.0 (neutral element of multiplication)\n    //   - binary_op = std::multiplies<double>()\n    //                             // init\n        std::multiplies<double>{},             // reduction operator\n        [&](std::size_t i) -> double            // transform\n        {\n            double v = x[i];\n            // odd index → invert, even index → keep as‑is\n            return (i & 1u) ? 1.0 / v : v;\n        });\n\n    return result;\n}\n```\n\n### Why this is fast\n\n* **Work‑sharing**
